Rufous motmot (Baryphthengus martii) is a large, strikingly colored member of the Momotidae family that inhabits the humid lowland forests of Central and South America. As an obligate cavity-nester, the species exhibits a life history strategy finely tuned to the seasonal availability of resources in its tropical environment. Under the warm thermal conditions typical of its active metabolic periods, specifically at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the eggs hatch after a relatively short incubation period of 20 days [ab = 20 days], a duration that is consistent with values reported for other mid-sized neotropical coraciiform birds. The newly emerged altricial chicks are notably small, with a neonatal body mass of 24 grams [Wwb = 24 grams], representing a minute fraction of the eventual adult size. This low birth weight of 24 grams [Wwb = 24 grams] necessitates an extended period of intensive parental provisioning. Field records from lowland Costa Rica indicate that the nestling phase unfolds predictably at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], with the downy chicks achieving their first flight and departing the nest cavity at 25 days since birth [tx = 25 days since birth], a developmental schedule that balances the risks of nest predation against the energetic demands of feather growth and muscle maturation.

The transition to nutritional independence following nest departure marks a critical period in the life cycle of juvenile Rufous motmots. Fledglings must rapidly develop proficient foraging skills to capture the large arthropods and small vertebrates that constitute their diet. The attainment of full reproductive capacity occurs later, with puberty being documented at 75 days since birth [tp = 75 days since birth] when individuals are maintained at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], a timing that allows for the completion of skeletal growth before the onset of gonadal activity. This age at sexual maturity is relatively rapid for a bird of this body size and likely reflects the high metabolic turnover characteristic of tropical insectivores. Young birds then undergo a gradual process of plumage maturation, transitioning from the duller juvenile plumage to the distinctive rufous underparts, green upperparts, and elongated central tail rectrices typical of the breeding adult. The sub-adult period serves as a crucial learning phase during which territory acquisition and pair bond formation are initiated, with the first successful breeding attempt typically occurring after an extended period of social and ecological preparation.

Females of Baryphthengus martii ultimately reach a definitive adult body mass of 155.7 grams [Wwi = 155.7 grams], a figure derived from measurements of asymptotically grown individuals in wild populations. This ultimate wet weight is towards the lower end of the documented range for the species, as standard field guides often report a broader span of 185 to 193 grams for general adult mass, suggesting considerable intraspecific variation related to local habitat quality and seasonal fat deposition. Males, by contrast, tend to achieve a slightly larger maximum adult mass of 159.2 grams [Wwi = 159.2 grams], a modest degree of sexual size dimorphism that is common among momotids and may be linked to the greater physical demands of cavity excavation. These asymptotic masses are achieved through a period of sustained growth during the nestling and early juvenile phases, after which the birds transition to a state of body mass maintenance where energy intake primarily supports daily metabolic costs and reproductive investment rather than continued structural increase.

Reproductive output in the Rufous motmot is constrained by the species' reliance on natural tree cavities and the limited duration of favorable nesting conditions in the wet season. Females produce 3 to 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 3 to 5 eggs per clutch], a typical fecundity for a tropical forest coraciiform, and typically raise a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year] when the ambient temperature averages 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This modest annual reproductive rate is a characteristic feature of a slow-paced life history strategy, where each nesting attempt represents a significant energetic investment in terms of both egg production and the prolonged period of biparental care required to bring the altricial young to independence. The energy allocated to each egg must be substantial enough to support the embryo's full development within the calcareous shell, and the resulting investment per offspring is therefore considerable. Comparative data from congeners suggest that this single-brooded pattern is stable across the genus, reflecting a consistent evolutionary trade-off between current reproductive effort and adult survival.

Under the stable thermal conditions typical of the species (40 °C [T = 40 °C]), the maximum lifespan recorded for the Rufous motmot under natural conditions is 12.7 years [am = 12.7 years], a longevity that aligns well with expectations for a bird of its size and tropical distribution. The physiological underpinnings of this extended lifespan are reflected in a resting metabolic rate of 100 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 100 milliliters of oxygen per hour], representing the standard energetic cost of sustaining vital functions in a thermoneutral state at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This value of basal oxygen consumption provides a baseline for understanding the species' daily energetic requirements. The initiation of the first reproductive effort is delayed substantially, with first successful breeding typically recorded at 584 days since birth [tR = 584 days since birth] at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This deferred onset, nearly 1.6 years after hatching, is a significant fraction of the total lifespan and reflects the extended period needed for cavity acquisition, pair formation, and the accumulation of sufficient foraging experience to support the energetic demands of egg production and chick provisioning.
